1.pericope_label: Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help, and stay on horses ... yet he also is wise, and will bring evil ... now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit
debates: How far lawful means may be used: Calvin insists that God does not disapprove of customary and lawful remedies, and locates the fault in an attachment to them that leaves God unsought.
What tone the second verse carries: Ellicott hears sarcasm allowing the counsellors their worldly wisdom, Gill and Wesley take it as a plain comparison of wisdom and strength.
outliers: Clarke reports a singular reading, his word, in two manuscripts and two versions, and one manuscript giving his ways.
Clarke identifies the helper as Egypt and the helped as Israel, both falling together.
themes: Trust divided between God and creatures
The wisdom that takes the wise in their craftiness

4.pericope_label: Like as the lion and the young lion roaring on his prey ... so shall the Lord of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion ... as birds flying, so will the Lord of hosts defend Jerusalem
debates: Whether the Lord comes down for Zion or against it: Ellicott lays out both renderings of the preposition, with the lion either defending its own or claiming its prey, and leans to protection because of the verse that follows.

What the closing verb means: Clarke rejects the received notion of skipping over the marked houses and argues for a springing forward to cover the door against the destroyer, while Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch note only the link to the festival.
outliers: Clarke prints a passage of Homer beside the lion simile and another beside the bird simile, and reports a Greek manuscript reading that gives going about he shall protect.
Gill hears the bird image sharpened by the invader’s own boast of having found the riches of the peoples like a nest.
themes: The lion that will not give up its own

6.pericope_label: Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted. For in that day every man shall cast away his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which your own hands have made unto you for a sin
debates: How the first clause construes: Calvin rejects the reading that makes the depth of the revolt a reason for returning and takes it as a measure, return according as you have deeply revolted.
Whether the casting away of idols is a promise of sincere reformation or only a prediction that men will discard what has failed them: Henry reports both and takes the first.
outliers: Clarke notes that all the ancient versions put the verb of revolting in the second person, and reports the last word omitted by the Greek, supplied from other copies, and taken by one scholar as an epithet giving your sinful hands.
themes: Conversion as the sum of the prophet’s teaching

8.pericope_label: Then shall the Assyrian fall with the sword, not of a mighty man ... and he shall pass over to his strong hold for fear ... saith the Lord, whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem
debates: What the sword of no mighty and no mean man means: Ellicott, Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch take it of a stroke wholly divine, while Clarke reads it historically of the king killed by his own sons, who were no soldiers but were princes.
How the opening of the last verse construes: Gill offers both the king passing over to his stronghold and his rock passing away for fear, and Ellicott rules for the second on the laws of parallelism.

What the fire in Zion is: Ellicott and Wesley take it for the divine glory that warms the faithful and burns the evil, Calvin renders it that God shall be a fire to the Assyrian and rejects the reading that refers it to the sacrifices.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject the old Greek and Latin rendering that reads a negative with the fleeing, and note the article withheld from the sword to suggest something unbounded.
themes: A deliverance with no human instrument
Repentance as the turn of the siege
Fire kindled in the midst of the people
